chapters.title: The pencil that seems to snap

lines.cap: Dip a straight pencil into a glass of water, and it suddenly looks **snapped in half**.
Pull it out, and it's perfectly whole. So what is happening to the light on its way to your eye?
This is the science of **light**: how it travels, bounces, bends, and splits into colours.
We'll draw ray diagrams, find out why a red apple looks red, and see how your own **eye** turns light into a picture.

chapters.title: How light travels and how we see

lines.cap: **Light** is a form of energy, and it travels in **straight lines**.
We draw its path as a **ray**: a straight line with an arrow showing which way it goes. A wide beam is just lots of rays.
And light is astonishingly fast: about **300,000 kilometres per second**, or **3 × 10⁸ m/s**.
That's fast enough to circle the Earth **seven and a half times** in one second.
It's about a **million times faster than sound**, which is why you see a firework burst before you hear the bang.
A **luminous** object **makes its own light**: the Sun, a lamp, a flame, a glowing screen.
A **non-luminous** object makes no light of its own: a book, an apple, even you.
So how do we see it? **We see an object when light reflects off it and enters our eye.**
Light goes from the source, to the object, into your eye. Your eyes don't send anything out; they only **receive** light.
And the Moon? It looks bright, but it's **non-luminous**. It simply reflects sunlight.
Materials treat light differently. **Transparent** ones let light pass straight through, so you can see clearly through them: clear glass, air, water.
**Translucent** ones let some light through, but **scatter** it, so you see light but not a sharp image: frosted glass, tracing paper, thin curtains.
And **opaque** ones let **no light** through at all: wood, metal, a brick wall.
Light travels in straight lines, so an opaque object **blocks** it. That leaves a **shadow**: a dark region, roughly the same shape as the object.
A tiny **point source** of light gives a shadow with a **sharp** edge.
A large source gives a fuzzy edge: a fully dark middle, the **umbra**, and a partly lit fringe, the **penumbra**.
Move the object **closer to the source**, and the shadow gets **bigger**, because it blocks a wider spread of rays.
Straight-line rays also explain why your shadow is short at midday, when the Sun is high, and long at sunset, when it's low.

chapters.title: Reflection and the law of reflection

lines.cap: When light hits a surface, it **reflects**: it bounces off.
To describe it, we draw the **normal**: an imaginary line at **90°** to the surface, right where the ray hits.
We always measure angles **from the normal**, never from the surface.
The ray arriving is the **incident ray**. The ray leaving is the **reflected ray**.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal is the **angle of incidence**, **i**.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal is the **angle of reflection**, **r**.
**The law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.** So i = r.
Tilt the incoming ray, and the reflected ray swings to match. Thirty degrees in, thirty degrees out.
To draw it, use a dashed normal and arrows on the rays, and measure **i** and **r** from the normal.
A smooth, shiny surface like a mirror gives **regular reflection**. Parallel rays stay parallel, so you see a clear image.
A rough surface like paper gives **diffuse reflection**. Its tiny bumps face different ways, so the rays **scatter** in all directions.
That's why a wall isn't a mirror. Yet diffuse reflection lets you see most objects from **any angle**.
A **plane mirror** is just a flat mirror. So where is the image you see in it?
Take two rays from the tip of a candle flame. Each one reflects off the mirror with equal angles.
The reflected rays spread apart. Extend them **backwards**, as dashed lines, and they meet behind the mirror. That's where the **image** is.
But no light really gets behind the mirror. The image is **virtual**: you can't catch it on a screen.
It's **as far behind the mirror** as the object is in front.
It's **upright**, the same way up, and the **same size** as the object.
And it's **laterally inverted**: left and right are swapped. Raise your right hand, and your reflection seems to raise its left.
That's why **AMBULANCE** is written back-to-front on the front of the vehicle, so it reads correctly in a driver's mirror.
But a mirror doesn't swap up and down. It really reverses **front to back**, and we see that as left and right swapped.
The four properties spell **VUSL**: Very Useful Smooth Looking-glass. **V**irtual, **U**pright, **S**ame size, **L**aterally inverted.

chapters.title: Refraction: light changes speed and bends

lines.cap: Light travels **more slowly** in denser materials, like glass and water, than in air.
When a ray crosses into a new material, or **medium**, at an angle, that change in speed makes it **bend**. This is **refraction**.
So light doesn't bend because it 'wants' a shortcut. It bends because its **speed changes**.
Going into a **denser** medium, like from air into glass, light **slows down** and bends **towards the normal**.
Going into a **less dense** medium, like from glass into air, it **speeds up** and bends **away from the normal**.
Remember: **SloTo, FastAway**. **Slo**w down, bend **to**wards. Go **fast**er, bend **away**.
But a ray that hits the boundary **along the normal** doesn't bend at all. It just changes speed.
That's what 'snaps' the pencil: light from the underwater part bends as it leaves the water, so that part looks **shifted**. Try it at home!
Refraction makes a swimming pool look **shallower** than it really is, and makes stars **twinkle**, as moving air refracts their light.
Now send a ray through a **rectangular glass block**. It refracts **twice**.
Going in, it slows down and bends **towards** the normal. Coming out, it speeds up and bends **away**, by exactly the same amount.
The block's faces are **parallel**, so the two bends are equal and opposite. The ray comes out **parallel** to the ray that went in.
It's just shifted **sideways**. That shift is called **lateral displacement**.
**White light**, like sunlight, isn't a single colour. It's a **mixture** of all the colours of the rainbow.
A **prism** is a triangular block of glass that refracts light at both faces. And it can pull those colours apart.
Each colour travels at a slightly different speed inside glass, so each refracts by a slightly different amount.
**Violet** bends the **most**, and **red** bends the **least**. The colours fan out into a band called the **visible spectrum**.
This splitting of white light is called **dispersion**.
From least bent to most bent: **red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet**.
To remember the order: **Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain**.
The prism doesn't **add** any colour. The colours were in the white light all along; the prism just **separates** them.
A **rainbow** is dispersion on a giant scale. Millions of raindrops each act like a tiny prism, refracting and reflecting sunlight back to you.
That's why you only see a rainbow with the **Sun behind you** and rain in front.
So why does a red apple look red? The colour you see depends on which colours of light **reach your eye**.
White light falls on the apple. The apple **reflects** the red light and **absorbs** all the other colours, so only red reaches you.
A green leaf reflects **green** and absorbs the rest.
A **white** object reflects **all** the colours. A **black** object absorbs them all, and reflects almost none.
So the apple doesn't glow, or turn the light red. It just **reflects** its own colour and **absorbs** the rest.
A **filter** is a piece of coloured, transparent material. It **transmits**, or lets through, its own colour, and **absorbs** the others.
Remember: **a filter is selfish**. It only lets its **own** colour through, so a red filter lets through only red light.
So look at a **blue** book through a red filter. The book reflects only blue light, the filter absorbs it, and the book looks **black**.
Under pure red light, a red shirt with a green logo looks red, but the logo looks **black**: there's no green light for it to reflect.
Your **eye** is a natural optical instrument. It focuses light to form an image.
Light enters through the **cornea**, the clear, curved front layer. The cornea does **most** of the bending.
Then it passes through the **pupil**, the black hole in the middle. It's not really a part: it's a **gap** that lets light in.
Around it is the **iris**, the coloured ring of muscle. It changes the pupil's size to control how much light gets in.
In bright light, the pupil is **small**. In dim light, it opens **wide**.
That's why a dark cinema looks pitch black when you first walk in: your pupils need a moment to widen.
Behind the pupil, the **lens** fine-tunes the focus.
The light lands on the **retina**, the light-sensitive layer at the back, where the image forms.
The cornea and lens bend the light so the rays meet on the retina. The image there is **real** and **inverted**: upside-down!
Cells in the retina send signals to your **brain**, which interprets the image the right way up.
If the image focuses in front of the retina, or behind it, things look blurry. **Glasses** bend the light so it focuses on the retina.

chapters.title: Focusing the eye: near and far

lines.cap: Your eye can switch focus from near to far in a moment, because its lens **changes shape**. This is called **accommodation**.
A ring of **ciliary muscles** surrounds the lens.
Fine fibres called **suspensory ligaments** join those muscles to the edge of the lens.
To focus on something **near**, the ciliary muscles **contract**. The ligaments go **slack**, and the lens becomes **fatter** and more curved, so it bends light **more**.
To focus on something **far away**, the ciliary muscles **relax**. The ligaments pull **tight** and stretch the lens **thinner** and flatter, so it bends light **less**.
Around it all is the **sclera**: the tough, white outer coat that protects the eye and holds its shape. It's the white of your eye.
At the back, the **optic nerve** carries electrical signals from the retina to your **brain**, which turns them into the picture you see.
Where the optic nerve leaves the retina, there are no light-sensitive cells. That spot is your **blind spot**.
The **primary colours of light** are **red, green and blue**. They're primary because you can't make them by mixing other lights.
Shine two of them onto the same spot, like stage spotlights, and they **add** together to make a new colour. This is **additive** mixing.
**Red + green = yellow.**
**Green + blue = cyan**, a greenish-blue.
**Red + blue = magenta**, a pinkish-purple.
And all **three** together make **white** light.
Yellow, cyan and magenta are the **secondary colours of light**.
That's how a phone or TV screen works. It has no yellow or white lights at all: just tiny **red, green and blue** dots.
By lighting them in different amounts, it makes every colour you see, even white.
It works because your eye senses colour with just three kinds of cells, called **cones**: red, green and blue. Your brain mixes their signals.
Mixing **paints** is the opposite. Each pigment **absorbs**, or subtracts, light, so mixing paints makes darker, muddier colours.
Back to glass. Light going from glass **out** into air mostly refracts out, bending away from the normal, but a little reflects back inside.
Make the angle of incidence inside the glass bigger, and the escaping ray bends further and further from the normal.
At one special angle, the refracted ray runs right **along the surface**. That's the **critical angle**: about **42°** for glass.
Go beyond it, and no light escapes at all. **All** of it reflects back inside, obeying the law of reflection. This is **total internal reflection**.
It needs **two conditions**. One: the light must be inside the **denser** material, heading for a less dense one, like glass to air.
Two: the angle of incidence must be **bigger than the critical angle**.
This is the secret of **optical fibres**: thin, flexible threads of very pure glass.
Light inside keeps hitting the walls at more than the critical angle, so it reflects again and again, **zig-zagging** along until it reaches the far end.
Fibres carry phone calls, TV and internet data as flashes of light, even under the oceans. And doctors use them in **endoscopes**, to see inside the body.
Diamonds sparkle for the same reason. Their critical angle is very small, so light bounces around inside before flashing back out.

chapters.title: Recap: memory hooks and exam traps

lines.cap: Let's lock it all in.
**Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain**: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
**SloTo, FastAway**: slow down, bend towards the normal; speed up, bend away.
**VUSL**: a plane-mirror image is virtual, upright, the same size, and laterally inverted.
**A filter is selfish**: it lets through only its own colour.
Now, five exam traps to avoid.
One: measure angles from the **normal**, never from the surface.
Two: a plane-mirror image is **virtual**, not real.
Three: light bends **towards** the normal only when it slows down, entering a denser medium. Leaving one, it bends away.
Four: in a prism, **violet** bends the most and **red** the least, not the other way round.
Five: the Moon is **non-luminous**. It only reflects sunlight.
Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
A light ray hits a mirror with an angle of incidence of 40°. What is the angle of reflection?
**40°**, because the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Light passes from air into glass at an angle. Which way does it bend?
**Towards the normal**, because it slows down.
What colour does a blue book look in pure red light?
**Black.** There's no blue light for it to reflect, and it absorbs the red.
Which two colours of light add together to make yellow?
**Red and green.**
True or false: the image on your retina is the right way up.
**False.** It's real and inverted, and your brain interprets it the right way up.
Brilliant work. Now try the Light & Optics quiz in your Science Lab, to lock it in.
